name: Raspberry ketones

card.summary: A raspberry-aroma compound sold as a fat burner; human weight-loss evidence is essentially absent and safety data are thin.
card.note: Sold as a supplement, but no regulator has approved it for weight loss and published human safety data are limited.

quick.overview:
Raspberry ketone is the main aroma molecule of red raspberries and is widely used as a flavouring and in perfumery. Supplements containing it, usually made synthetically, are marketed as fat burners.

Research on its weight-loss effect is mostly in rodents and cell cultures. Encyclopedic summaries state that no clinical evidence of weight loss in humans has been established.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it boosts fat breakdown and raises adiponectin or norepinephrine signalling. Laboratory studies in obese rats have reported changes in lipid levels, insulin resistance and adipose-tissue gene expression, including the water-and-glycerol channel aquaporin 7. A small registered human study (NCT06681597) examined circulating FGF21 and energy expenditure, but its results are not described in the sources available.
quick.risks: The US FDA classed raspberry ketone as generally recognised as safe only as a food flavouring in tiny amounts. Safety of supplement-level intake in people is poorly characterised. Case reports describe coronary vasospasm and ventricular tachycardia in people taking raspberry ketone weight-loss products, and a 2015 toxicology paper and a Danish university warning raised concerns about supplement use.

lead: Raspberry ketone (4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)butan-2-one, also called rheosmin or frambinone) is a phenolic compound that gives red raspberries much of their characteristic smell. It also occurs in cranberries and blackberries, and is used in perfumery, cosmetics and as a food flavouring. [1]

Because raspberries contain only a few milligrams per kilogram, commercial supplements generally rely on synthetically produced raspberry ketone. [1] Products are marketed for weight loss and fat burning, a use that grew from rodent studies on adipose tissue and lipid metabolism. [2]

Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence for a weight-loss effect in humans, and that no international regulatory authority has approved it as a weight-loss supplement. [1] Published case reports describe cardiac events in people taking such products, though a causal link has not been established. [3][4]

paras: Raspberry ketone is a white crystalline solid that the plant makes from coumaroyl-CoA. Natural extraction yields only about 1 to 4 mg per kilogram of fruit, so industrial supplies are made chemically, for example by condensing acetone with 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde and then hydrogenating the product. [1]
The word 'ketone' refers to the compound's carbonyl group. It is unrelated to the ketone bodies produced in ketosis, a point Wikipedia notes as a naming coincidence. [1]

Raspberry ketone is sold alone and in blends of supplements aimed at weight loss. Marketing has typically described it as a way to increase fat breakdown. A review of newer dietary supplements for obesity includes it among products whose popularity has outpaced human evidence. [5]

In an experiment in male obese rats, raspberry ketone was reported to lower body weight gain, hyperlipidemia and insulin resistance, with changes in adipocytokines and aquaporin 7 expression in fat tissue. [2] Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity has also been reported in mouse and rat models of chemotherapy-induced organ injury. [6][7]
A laboratory study of five berry products, including raspberry ketones, found only weak inhibition of several UDP-glucuronosyltransferase enzymes that metabolise drugs. [8]

No published randomised trial has established a weight-loss effect of raspberry ketone supplements in humans, according to Wikipedia's summary. [1] A registered early-phase human study (NCT06681597, 60 participants, completed) examined whether raspberry ketone intake raises circulating FGF21 and energy expenditure in people with obesity, diabetes or fatty liver. [9] A second registration lists raspberry ketone only as part of a diet study in 14 participants. [10] Most mechanistic work comes from rodents and cells. [2]

The FDA's 1965 GRAS status applies to its use as a flavouring in small quantities, not to supplement doses. [1] A 2015 paper by Bredsdorff and colleagues expressed concern about high intakes from supplements with few toxicity data, and the Technical University of Denmark issued a 2016 warning that such products may be harmful. [1]

A case report in the Anatolian Journal of Cardiology described coronary vasospasm in a person using a raspberry ketone weight-loss supplement, and a 2022 case report in Cureus described resistant polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in another. Both are single cases; neither establishes causation. [3][4]
No regulator has approved raspberry ketone as a weight-loss treatment. It is sold in many countries as a dietary supplement. [1]

timeline.event: US FDA classifies raspberry ketone as generally recognised as safe for use as a food flavouring. [1]
Bredsdorff and colleagues publish a paper raising safety concerns about high intakes from food supplements. [1]
The Technical University of Denmark warns that supplements containing raspberry ketone may be harmful. [1]
A 60-participant early-phase human study of raspberry ketone and FGF21 begins. [9]
